overview: The Achaemenid Empire, founded by Cyrus the Great in 550 BCE, was the largest state the world had seen, reaching from the Balkans and Egypt to the Indus. Its kings ruled dozens of peoples through satraps, roads and a common administrative language, and mostly let them keep their gods and laws.

items.text: The Royal Road ran about 2,700 kilometers from Susa to Sardis; Herodotus says a traveler took ninety days and a relay of royal couriers about a week.
Qanats, tunnels that carry groundwater out to the plains, spread across Iran under the empire.
Darius I struck the gold daric and the silver siglos, the first coins used across the whole empire.
Darius began Persepolis, with its terrace, hundred-columned halls, bull capitals and staircases carved with tribute-bearers from every province.
The Cyrus Cylinder, a clay text from Babylon, records Cyrus restoring temples and sending deported peoples home; the modern description of it as a charter of human rights is disputed by historians.
The kings invoked Ahura Mazda in their inscriptions; how far the court followed Zoroaster's teaching is debated.
Cyrus let the Judean exiles in Babylon return to Jerusalem and rebuild the Temple, as the Hebrew Bible records.
Some twenty satrapies paid tribute in silver and kind, each under a governor watched by the king's inspectors.
Roads, coinage and a long peace tied the Mediterranean to Central Asia and India.
Imperial Aramaic served as the language of administration from Egypt to Bactria.
Later Iranian dynasties, the Sasanians above all, looked back to the Achaemenids.
Alexander and the Seleucids kept the satrapies and much of the administration.

fall.text: Alexander defeated Darius III at Gaugamela in 331 BCE and burned Persepolis in 330. Darius was killed by his own satrap the same year, and Alexander took the empire as its heir.
